title: The rising cost of trade
gist: Oxford Economics cuts its global goods export growth forecast because higher bond yields, renewed inflation and a sharp oil-price rise are jointly raising the cost of trade: export growth is now seen troughing at 2.9% in Q1 2027 (vs 3.6% in the baseline published earlier the same month) and averaging 3% in 2027 (vs 3.5%). Firms are expected to respond by adjusting orders and inventories, with uneven effects on freight demand across cargo types and shipping segments.

insights.claim: Global trade is under simultaneous pressure from three forces arriving together in late 2026: higher bond yields, renewed inflation, and a sharp rise in oil prices.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Treat rates, CPI and crude as a combined trade-volume headwind rather than separate macro risks; trade-sensitive cyclicals face stacked pressure.
insights.locator: Higher bond yields, inflation, and oil prices are raising the cost of trade

insights.claim: Renewed inflation erodes household purchasing power while higher interest rates reduce spending, cutting final demand for traded goods.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Demand-side drag on import volumes argues for caution on consumer-goods exporters and import-dependent retailers while real incomes are squeezed.
insights.quote: Higher inflation erodes purchasing power and higher rates can reduce spending.
insights.locator: The impacts of these developments on trade are three-fold

insights.claim: Rising bond yields make trade financing more costly, adding a financial-conditions channel through which higher rates directly suppress cross-border goods flows.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Watch trade-finance spreads and working-capital costs for smaller exporters and EM traders; a yield back-up tightens trade before it shows in GDP.
insights.quote: Higher bond yields make trade financing more costly.
insights.locator: The impacts of these developments on trade are three-fold

insights.claim: Higher oil prices raise the cost of physically moving goods, acting as a direct tax on freight and logistics that dampens trade volumes.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Bunker-fuel pass-through squeezes shippers and logistics margins where contracts lag fuel costs; oil is now a trade-volume variable, not just an inflation one.
insights.quote: Higher oil prices raise the cost of moving goods.
insights.locator: The impacts of these developments on trade are three-fold

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' latest baseline sees global goods export growth troughing at 2.9% in Q1 2027, down from 3.6% in its previous baseline issued earlier in September 2026 — a 0.7pp cut within a single month.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The speed of the revision signals deteriorating momentum; consensus trade and freight forecasts made before mid-September likely need to come down.

insights.claim: The trade slowdown is expected to persist through all of 2027, with global goods export growth averaging 3% for the year versus a prior forecast of 3.5%.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Not a one-quarter air pocket: position for a full year of sub-trend trade growth in shipping, ports and export-heavy equity markets.

themes.theme: Orders, inventories and uneven freight demand

insights.claim: Firms are expected to respond to the higher cost of trade by adjusting orders and inventories, which will hit freight demand unevenly across cargo types and shipping segments rather than uniformly.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Differentiate within shipping: inventory destocking and order cuts hit segments differently, so segment selection (e.g. by cargo type) matters more than a blanket sector call.
insights.quote: Firms will respond by adjusting orders and inventories, with different implications for freight demand across cargo types and shipping segments.
insights.locator: Firms will respond by adjusting orders and inventories
